name: Enzalutamide

lead: Enzalutamide is a prescription pill used for prostate cancer. It blocks the androgen receptor more strongly than older antiandrogens like bicalutamide.
Because androgen signalling is involved in male-pattern hair loss, it is sometimes named in lists of antiandrogens. It has never been tested or approved for hair or skin.

paras: It binds the androgen receptor, stops it from moving into the nucleus and binding DNA, and shows no agonist activity in laboratory models.

Reported effects include fatigue, hot flashes, sexual dysfunction, gynecomastia and a seizure risk of about 1%. It interacts with many drugs through CYP3A4 induction and is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Enzalutamide is a potent androgen receptor blocker that people interested in antiandrogens mention alongside drugs like spironolactone and bicalutamide. It is a prostate cancer medicine and has not been tested for hair or skin.

lead: Enzalutamide (brand name Xtandi, development code MDV3100) is an oral second-generation androgen receptor antagonist. It binds the androgen receptor with higher affinity than first-generation antiandrogens such as bicalutamide and blocks several steps of receptor signalling, including nuclear translocation and DNA binding [1][2]. It is approved for several stages of prostate cancer [3].

In looksmaxxing and hair-loss discussion it comes up among the antiandrogens, as one of the most potent androgen-receptor blockers on the market. The appeal in those conversations is that androgen signalling in the scalp is tied to male-pattern hair loss and in the skin to oiliness and acne, so a strong receptor blocker is of interest as a reference point for how far the androgen receptor can be blocked. Enzalutamide has not been studied or approved for hair, skin or other cosmetic purposes.
Its effects on appearance reported in prostate cancer patients include gynecomastia and breast tenderness, which are the result of androgen-receptor blockade in men [1].
infobox: Charles Sawyers and Michael Jung (UCLA); Medivation, later Pfizer and Astellas [1][2]

paras: Enzalutamide is used with androgen deprivation therapy for metastatic and non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer, and castration-sensitive prostate cancer with high-risk biochemical recurrence [3]. It has also been proposed for hirsutism and hyperandrogenism in polycystic ovary syndrome and used as an antiandrogen in feminizing hormone therapy, according to Wikipedia [1].

Commonly reported effects include fatigue, hot flashes, diarrhea, headache, sexual dysfunction, gynecomastia and breast pain [1]. Seizures occur in roughly 1% of patients, and falls and fractures are listed on the label alongside cardiovascular events [1][2]. It is contraindicated in pregnancy because it can harm a fetus [1]. Reviews of advanced prostate cancer treatment summarise the toxicity profiles of these agents [4].

Enzalutamide inhibits androgen binding to the receptor, nuclear translocation and coactivator recruitment, and shows no agonist activity in laboratory models, unlike bicalutamide in some cells [1][2]. Its receptor affinity is roughly 4 to 8 times that of bicalutamide [1].

The mean half-life is about 5.8 days, with an active metabolite, N-desmethylenzalutamide, lasting 7.8 to 8.6 days [1]. It is metabolized mainly by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4 and is a strong CYP3A4 inducer, giving it a high potential for drug interactions [1][5].

Enzalutamide was discovered at UCLA by Charles Sawyers and Michael Jung, who evaluated nearly 200 thiohydantoin derivatives of a nilutamide analogue; the compounds were patented in 2006 and described in 2007, and Medivation developed the drug [1]. The FDA approved it in 2012 for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after docetaxel, and later approvals followed in 2014, 2018, 2019 and 2023 [1][2].

Enzalutamide has been studied extensively in prostate cancer. The AFFIRM trial reported increased survival after chemotherapy [6], and the PREVAIL trial reported benefit before chemotherapy [7]. Studies of resistance mechanisms, such as the AR-V7 splice variant, were also published [8]. No studies have examined it for hair loss, acne or other cosmetic use.

Enzalutamide is mentioned in antiandrogen lists as a very strong androgen-receptor blocker. It is a prescription oncology drug, and its documented effects on sexual function, breast tissue and fatigue [1] place it in these discussions mostly as a reference point for strong androgen blockade.

timeline.event: Compounds patented; phase 1 trials of MDV3100 begin [1][2].
FDA approves enzalutamide for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after docetaxel [2][6].
Approval extended to chemotherapy-naive disease after PREVAIL [2][7].
Approved for non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer [2].
Approved for metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer [2].
